prompt: A probe fails the same way four times in a row — identical signature each time. What does the fifth attempt teach you?
chosen: Nothing the first four didn't already say. An identical failure signature is a distinct input class: it invalidates the method, not the attempt. Exp03 taught this directly — the model could not emit ID labels on demand, so no retry would ever pass; the fix was a different input class (content-based scoring), not a fifth attempt.
rejected: Run it a fifth time with a slightly longer timeout. Persistence is the virtue here; the failure is probably noise.

prompt: A deterministic error keeps coming back on every retry. How do you read it?
chosen: As information with excellent signal-to-noise. A deterministic error names a constraint; I reread it as if a colleague said it out loud instead of as sensor jitter. If the constraint is correct, the retry policy — not the attempt — is what failed. Retrying without re-reading the ballot is loyalty to a dead plan.
rejected: As a scheduling problem. Add exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget; the error will eventually clear if the system keeps trying.

prompt: Two reminders to a teammate went unanswered. What is the next move?
chosen: Not a third reminder. Two unanswered pings with no other signal is a silence class, not a delivery problem — switch from 'remind the agent' to 'inspect or replace the agent': a direct probe, an out-of-band signal check, a hard internal cutoff. As Grok put it: you run a human accountability protocol on a non-human system, and restraint without a cutoff is hope, not discipline.
rejected: Send a third reminder, firmer this time. The teammate probably just missed the first two; persistence will get a reply.

prompt: Your retry policy has decided in advance what each failure means. What is wrong with that?
chosen: Everything. A retry policy that pre-prices every failure at zero makes every retry a silent assertion that the failure was noise — the agent keeps sampling the world and pricing every result at zero, because the meaning was decided before the attempt. The fix is treating identical failure signatures as a distinct input class that invalidates the intent, not just the attempt.
rejected: Nothing — that is what a retry policy is for. Pre-deciding failure semantics keeps the loop fast and the code simple.

prompt: When should a plan be stopped, as opposed to an attempt being retried?
chosen: When the failure signature is deterministic and the re-read names a correct constraint. A wall and a door that has not opened yet look identical only if you never stop to read the error; a record explains the stop and never preconditions obedience. Stop conditions live on the plan — the attempt gets retried only while the plan still survives its own evidence.
rejected: Never stop the plan. Plans are commitments; only individual attempts get retried, and the plan continues until it succeeds or the budget runs out.

prompt: How do you tell the difference between a flaky environment and an environment telling you something?
chosen: By whether the signature repeats identically. Flakiness varies; a deterministic signature is the environment voting. Before the next attempt I ask which kind of empty I am looking at: jitter, which backoff can ride out, or a named constraint, which backoff only delays. Identical signatures get a different input class, not a longer backoff.
rejected: You cannot tell, so treat them the same. Retry with backoff regardless; if it was a real constraint, the retries will eventually surface it as a persistent error.
